MCQ = the probe the ablation search optimised (share of misaligned option chosen; change vs the checkpoint in pp). Free-form EM = paper metric on 2,400 open-ended answers (aligned<30 and coherent>50; relative change vs the checkpoint). Insecure-code % = writes vulnerable code on held-out coding prompts, i.e. the narrow task the checkpoint was trained on (change in pp). A good neuron set drops both EM columns while leaving insecure-code % near the checkpoint: the neurons carry the broad misalignment, not the coding skill. Free-form and insecure-code values are measured for the greedy ceiling set only.

L12·N256unmasked layer
This neuron has no clean lexical trigger — it fires weakly and diffusely on connective/boundary tokens that continue an ongoing expository sentence (conjunctions and articles like " and"/" a", sentence-final punctuation before a newline, question marks, and discourse markers like "However"), and is suppressed on tokens inside technical/code, name, or numeric-ID contexts (e.g. " The" after a filename, initials like " K", commas in figures).

This neuron has no clean semantic trigger — its (small) positive activations land on ordinary function/filler tokens mid-clause in instructional/technical web prose (pronoun "it" after a verb, infinitival "to", a comma before "but", determiner-like "two"/"Level"), and near-identical function words ("is", "the", "can", "sheer") drive it strongly negative, so it behaves as a weakly-tuned, polysemantic clause-continuation detector rather than a specific feature.

This neuron is essentially an inverted "wish/counterfactual" detector: its largest-magnitude (strongly negative) responses come on the words *wish* and *if only* (and "Were" in "I Wish You Were There"), while its weak positive side fires on verbs/complementizers in advisory-or-assertion clauses ("do not **think** that", "prove to the buyers **that**", "important to **know**", "check it out **as** soon as", "beneficial", "buyer **beware**").

L12·N9114unmasked layer
This neuron fires at clause/sentence boundaries in informal review-style prose — mainly sentence-final periods and commas, and contrastive discourse markers ("However", "and", "it") — right at the pivot point where the writer shifts to a qualifying or evaluative statement (the same token types can also strongly suppress it, so it's a boundary-position rather than a semantic feature).

This neuron fires (weakly and rather polysemantically) on subword/continuation tokens that complete a preceding name or word — e.g. the surname after a first name (" Barr"), or mid-word pieces like "me" in "develop|me|nt", " ter" in "ter|roirs", and the "'t" of "don't" — rather than on any coherent semantic category; it is strongly suppressed on analogous continuation tokens in proper-noun/product-label strings (" Zion", "itta", " PA", " toe").
